::: {.kw-overview}
Supply and its efficient use dominate this issue. A very large US registry analysis shows that deceased-donor kidney offers are strikingly concentrated — a small minority of candidates absorb the majority of offers — pointing to an allocation inefficiency that offer filters and active waitlist management might correct, while a companion UNOS study confirms that priority for prior living donors shortens waits but leaves more than half already on dialysis before listing and exposes a racial gap in pre-transplant dialysis time. Donor-pool expansion features again in a single-centre report that a shortened four-week direct-acting antiviral course reliably clears hepatitis C when viraemic-donor kidneys go to seronegative recipients. Immunology and biomarkers run as a second thread: preformed HLA-DQ donor-specific antibodies emerge as treatment-resistant drivers of late antibody-mediated rejection, Torque Teno Virus load is refined into risk-prediction models for rejection and infection, and simple waist-based triglyceride-glucose indices predict new-onset diabetes, graft failure and death. The issue closes on graft-preserving care — therapeutic plasma exchange for recurrent focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, where earlier and more prolonged treatment favours remission — and on the perioperative case for robot-assisted transplantation, which lowers blood loss and wound complications at the cost of longer ischaemia times while matching open surgery for graft and patient survival.
:::

### 1. [Kidney Transplant Candidates With High Frequency Deceased Donor Offers.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2026.106611)
[Schold JD, Arrigain S, Husain SA, Yu M, Lopez R, Brosi D, LaVanchy R, Pshak T, Cooper J, Nydam T, Mohan S. *Kidney Int Rep*, 2026. PMID: 42328684.]{.kw-ref}

This retrospective observational study used the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients to map how deceased-donor kidney offers are distributed across the US waiting list, analysing 7,608,578 offers made to 205,780 kidney-only candidates between January 2021 and December 2024, with an average of 19.4 months of follow-up. The distribution was highly skewed: the median candidate received 17 offers (interquartile range 6–46), yet 28% of all offers went to just 5% of candidates and 55% went to the 15% designated high-frequency candidates, who each fielded at least 74 offers over the period. In multivariable models these high-frequency candidates were independently more likely to be aged 50–59 (incidence rate ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.24–1.29 versus 18–39), male (1.14), Black (1.30 versus White), of blood group O (1.69 versus type A) and to have a body mass index of 35 kg/m² or more (1.12), while the highly sensitised and those with the longest pre-listing dialysis received far fewer offers. There was wide between-centre variation, with the proportion of high-frequency candidates ranging from a median of 9% (IQR 2–17%) up to 42%, and a hierarchical model returned a median incidence rate ratio of 3.18 — meaning offers were more than tripled simply by being listed at a high-proportion centre, implicating centre practice beyond patient characteristics. Centres with more high-frequency candidates had lower transplant rates and lower offer acceptance ratios and were more likely to be flagged as underperforming, and these candidates ultimately received kidneys from older deceased and living donors when they were transplanted. The authors caution that the design is non-causal, that offers were restricted to kidneys eventually transplanted, that reasons for repeated declines were not captured, and that high-frequency candidates by definition wait longer, which confounds their apparently lower transplant and mortality rates. For UK practice, where allocation efficiency and rising organ non-utilisation are live concerns, it argues for systematically identifying candidates with repeated declines, using individualised offer filters, and revisiting active status so that scarce organs are directed to candidates genuinely ready to accept them.

### 2. [Keeping Our Promise: Expedited Allocation for Prior Living Kidney Donors and Trends in Waiting Times According to Race.](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70618)
[Mujtahedi SS, McCracken E, Webb C, Whittington O, Farney A, Orlando G, Casingal V, Stratta RJ, Jay C. *Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42525482.]{.kw-ref}

This national UNOS analysis examined whether the allocation priority given to prior living kidney donors who themselves later need a transplant translates into faster access, and whether that benefit is shared equitably by race. Comparing prior living donors with matched controls, the transplant rate was 86.2 versus 20.4 per 100 person-years (p < 0.001), such that 83% of prior donors were transplanted against 50% of controls, and median waiting time was dramatically shorter at 93 days (IQR 27–371) versus 692 days (233–1351). The priority effect strengthened after the 2014 Kidney Allocation System, with donor waiting time falling from 133 to 67 days (p < 0.001). Despite this, the safety net was imperfect: 56% of prior donors were already on dialysis before listing and 61% before transplant (versus 66% and 82% of controls), and time on dialysis did not improve meaningfully in the post-policy era (547 to 461 days, p = 0.06). Waiting times were broadly comparable across racial groups, but Black prior donors were more often on dialysis at listing (61% versus 52% of White donors, p = 0.02) and spent 36% longer on dialysis — an extra 155 days (p = 0.0002). As a retrospective registry study grounded in US allocation rules, its numbers do not transfer directly to the UK offering scheme. Nonetheless it reinforces a principle relevant to any programme that grants prior donors priority: the priority works, but the high proportion already dialysis-dependent before listing underscores the need for structured long-term donor follow-up, earlier re-referral, and attention to the residual racial gap in timely access.

### 3. [Outcomes After 4-Week Course of Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir Therapy in Hepatitis C Seronegative Recipients of Kidneys From Hepatitis C Viremic Deceased Donors.](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70629)
[Kummangal BA, Hack M, Selvam SA, Connelly C, Smith J, Pandav J, Mattos A, Do L, Ziolko A, McKenna D, Rehman S. *Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42530567.]{.kw-ref}

Transplanting kidneys from hepatitis C viraemic deceased donors into seronegative recipients expands the donor pool, but the optimal duration of direct-acting antiviral prophylaxis remains undefined, and this single-centre retrospective review tested a shortened 28-day course. Fifty HCV-seronegative adults who received a kidney from an HCV nucleic-acid-test-positive deceased donor at a Veterans Affairs centre between September 2017 and March 2025 were given sofosbuvir/velpatasvir prophylaxis for 28 days; the cohort was mostly older men (mean age 62.8 years, 92% male) receiving moderately marginal organs (mean kidney donor profile index 59.8). The primary endpoint, sustained virologic response 12 weeks after completing prophylaxis, was achieved in 46 of 50 (92%), with two of these requiring extension to a 12-week course for transient viraemia. Four patients (8%) failed prophylaxis but all cleared the virus with standard treatment, giving 100% overall sustained virologic response. One-year outcomes were reassuring: delayed graft function in 16%, biopsy-proven acute rejection in 12%, CMV viraemia in 18%, BK viraemia in 16%, mean estimated glomerular filtration rate of 57.7 ml/min/1.73m², no direct-acting-antiviral-attributable adverse events and 2% all-cause mortality unrelated to hepatitis C. Older age (72.3 versus 62.0 years, p = 0.030) and higher estimated post-transplant survival scores (86.5 versus 61.8, p = 0.041) were associated with prophylaxis failure, suggesting a subgroup that may need longer cover or closer surveillance. The evidence is limited by its small, single-centre, predominantly male composition and retrospective design. For UK units weighing HCV-viraemic-donor programmes, it supports a pragmatic short prophylactic course paired with HCV RNA monitoring and a low threshold to extend or treat, while flagging that the oldest, highest-risk recipients merit particular vigilance.

### 4. [Preformed HLA-DQ Donor-Specific Antibodies: Distinct Immunological Characteristics and Clinical Implications in Kidney Transplantation.](https://doi.org/10.1111/tan.70868)
[Lee H, Yoon J, Kim B, Park H, Eum SH, Lee S, Min JW, Ban TH, Yoon HE, Oh EJ, Chung BH. *HLA*, 2026. PMID: 42528174.]{.kw-ref}

This single-centre retrospective study set out to characterise preformed HLA-DQ donor-specific antibodies and their consequences, drawing on 1,540 ABO-compatible kidney transplant recipients with high-resolution HLA typing at a Korean centre between January 2010 and December 2024, of whom 179 carried preformed donor-specific antibodies. Patients were split into a DQ group (n = 58, those with DQ antibodies alone or combined with others) and a non-DQ group (n = 121), and the authors compared baseline antibody features, desensitisation response and post-transplant course. The DQ group contained proportionately more re-transplant recipients and their antibodies carried markedly higher baseline mean fluorescence intensity, and they proved far more refractory to desensitisation — 45.2% of DQ antibodies remained strong (mean fluorescence intensity above 10,000) afterwards, compared with only 2.8% of non-DQ antibodies. Although the overall incidence of acute antibody-mediated rejection did not differ significantly between groups, its timing and mechanism did: late-onset rejection was much more common in the DQ group (41.7% versus 10.0%, p = 0.024) and developed in the presence of persisting preformed DQ antibodies, whereas the DQ group's early rejections arose only after preformed antibodies had cleared. Allograft function also declined more rapidly in DQ-sensitised recipients. As a single-centre retrospective series it establishes association rather than a treatment pathway, and the DQ subgroup is modest in size. For UK practice it strengthens the case that preformed DQ antibodies are a distinct, treatment-resistant, high-risk category demanding more stringent long-term antibody surveillance and tailored, sustained immunosuppression rather than reassurance from an uneventful early post-transplant period.

### 5. [Predictive models for graft rejection and infections in renal transplant patients based on TTV viral load.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcv.2026.105969)
[Reyes NS, Poletta FA, Jara R, Boccia N, Díaz C, Soler Pujol G, Hermida E, Laham G, Echavarria M. *J Clin Virol*, 2026. PMID: 42398370.]{.kw-ref}

Torque Teno Virus is a ubiquitous, non-pathogenic virus whose blood level tracks the net state of immunosuppression, and this study asked whether quantifying it could predict the two dominant complications of over- and under-immunosuppression: rejection and opportunistic infection. The investigators measured TTV viral load in 871 plasma samples from 130 renal transplant recipients followed for up to three years and built logistic-regression models, contrasting a basal model using TTV load alone against an enhanced model adding patient variables, with performance judged by area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve. TTV was highly prevalent, detected in 81.2% of patients before transplantation and 97.6% by month three, while the cohort experienced a 36.6% rate of clinical or subclinical rejection and a 55.4% rate of infection. TTV load alone discriminated poorly for rejection (area under the curve 0.595) and modestly for infection (0.662), but the enhanced models improved substantially to 0.781 and 0.765 respectively. At their operating points the enhanced models reached a sensitivity and specificity of 61.1% and 81.8% for rejection and 81.8% and 68.7% for infection, with high negative predictive values of 97.7% and 94.3%, and internal validation reproduced these figures. The study is limited to a single cohort with internal validation only, and TTV alone added little for rejection prediction. For UK practice it adds to the accumulating signal that TTV monitoring, combined with routine clinical variables, could help rule out impending rejection and infection given the high negative predictive values, but external and prospective validation is needed before it could inform immunosuppression decisions.

### 6. [Anthropometry-adjusted TyG indices predict diabetes, graft failure, and mortality in kidney transplant recipients.](https://doi.org/10.1210/jendso/bvag157)
[Xiong J, Szili-Torok T, Özyilmaz ÖT, Xu W, Daamen JS, Jonker J, Groothof D, Kremer D, Neto AG, Pol RA, de Borst MH, Bakker SJL. *J Endocr Soc*, 2026. PMID: 42482953.]{.kw-ref}

The triglyceride-glucose index is a cheap surrogate for insulin resistance, and this prospective observational study asked which of its many variants best predicts hard outcomes after kidney transplantation. Working within the Dutch TransplantLines Biobank and Cohort, the authors followed 464 recipients with a functioning graft (median age 56.9 years, 65.1% male) for a median of 71 months and compared 15 triglyceride-glucose-derived indices — grouped as metabolic, anthropometry-adjusted or variability-based — for their ability to predict new-onset diabetes after transplantation, graft failure and all-cause mortality, using a framework combining machine learning with conventional statistics. Four indices stood out (TyG-WWI, TyG-WHR, TyG mean and TyG-BMI), and the two anthropometry-adjusted, waist-based measures gave the most stable signal across all three outcomes. In multivariable analysis TyG-WHR independently predicted new-onset diabetes (hazard ratio 2.30, 95% CI 1.21–4.39), graft failure (2.22, 1.18–4.18) and mortality (1.87, 1.19–2.96), while TyG-WWI independently predicted mortality (2.07, 1.11–3.86), and combining indices offered no consistent advantage over a single well-chosen one. The authors note the findings come from a single, relatively homogeneous cohort and require validation in larger and more diverse populations. For UK practice, where cardiometabolic disease and post-transplant diabetes are major long-term threats, it suggests that a waist-circumference-based triglyceride-glucose index — computed from data already collected in clinic — could be a low-cost way to flag recipients at higher risk of diabetes, graft loss and death, pending external validation.

### 7. [Outcomes in Recurrent Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis Post-Kidney Transplantation Treated With Therapeutic Plasma Exchange: A Retrospective Cohort Study.](https://doi.org/10.1002/jca.70156)
[Okwuonu CG, Hassan MO, Ojo OE, Virmani S, Balogun RA. *J Clin Apher*, 2026. PMID: 42420200.]{.kw-ref}

Recurrent focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is a leading cause of allograft loss and the efficacy of apheresis is poorly defined, so this retrospective cohort examined outcomes and predictors of response to therapeutic plasma exchange. Twenty adults with a pre-transplant diagnosis of the disease who developed biopsy-confirmed recurrence between January 2017 and December 2022 and were treated with plasma exchange were analysed, encompassing 169 exchange sessions. Fifteen of the twenty (75%) achieved remission of proteinuria while five (25%) did not, with a median time to remission of six months and a median of seven exchange sessions (interquartile range 2–13); there was no significant difference in time to remission between complete and partial responders. Two factors independently predicted remission: receiving more than five exchange sessions (adjusted odds ratio 1.6, 95% CI 1.01–2.46; p = 0.02) and lower baseline proteinuria at the start of treatment (adjusted odds ratio 1.9, 95% CI 1.03–8.94; p = 0.01). The procedure was well tolerated, with a 10.7% complication rate led by hypocalcaemia (5.9%), and a single death during apheresis gave a procedure mortality of 0.6%. As a small, single-centre retrospective series without a comparator, its estimates are directional and its wide confidence intervals reflect the modest sample. For UK practice it supports initiating plasma exchange early — while proteinuria is still relatively low — and persisting beyond the initial induction phase to capture late responders, while maintaining vigilance for the electrolyte and vascular-access complications of apheresis.

### 8. [Robot-assisted versus open kidney transplantation: an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-026-03677-y)
[Madi R, Helou E. *J Robot Surg*, 2026. PMID: 42503574.]{.kw-ref}

This umbrella review synthesised the existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses comparing robot-assisted with open kidney transplantation, following PRISMA methodology and appraising the quality of the underlying reviews with the AMSTAR-2 tool. Six reviews met inclusion criteria — four meta-analyses and two systematic reviews — all judged to be of low to moderate methodological quality, and they collectively covered a broad panel of perioperative and outcome measures including ischaemia times, blood loss, wound complications, graft function and survival. Robot-assisted surgery was associated with better perioperative outcomes across several domains: less blood loss (mean differences ranging from −16 to −55 ml across the studies), reduced post-operative pain, shorter incision length, fewer surgical site infections and fewer ureteral leaks. Open surgery, conversely, was favoured for cold ischaemia time, rewarming time, total ischaemia time, operative time and rate of ileus — a coherent trade-off reflecting the additional intracorporeal manipulation the robotic approach entails. Crucially, the harder endpoints of graft rejection, graft failure, all-cause mortality and hospital readmission were equivalent between the two techniques. The authors are explicit that the low-to-moderate quality of the source reviews limits confidence and that high-quality prospective studies are still needed. For UK centres considering or expanding robot-assisted kidney transplantation — particularly for obese or living-donor recipients where the wound and blood-loss advantages are most valuable — it offers measured reassurance that graft and patient survival are not compromised, while making clear that longer ischaemia times remain the principal price to weigh.
